div.p: This paper deals with the deployment ofindustrial control applications on distributed execution supports. These applications are developed according to the IEC 61499 standard. They are based on compositions of event triggered components. The execution support is a network of computational units scheduling OS tasks. The deployment problem consists then in associating components execu- tions to OS tasks. We resolve this problem by proposing a method based on a heuristic and a schedulability analysis. This method has to take into account the execution support limitation while satisfying functional and temporal constraints on application components.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: In several industrial sectors, the development of dis- tributed control applications is not an obvious activity [1]. Indeed, these applications have to verify functional and extra-functional [2] properties. One of these properties deals with the real-time behavior [3].
In addition, the realization time between the specification and the commercialization of a safety control application becomes more shorter.
To address all these constraints, the component approach can be exploited [4]. This approach supports reusability of already developed components.

Several component based approaches have been proposed to develop industrial control applications [4]. The IEC 61499 standard [5,6] is a well known approach al- lowing to design control applications as well as their exe- cution supports [7].
According to the standard, a Function Block (FB) is a reusable and event triggered component. A control application is a network of FBs distributed on devices.

A device contains one or more resources. A resource is considered as a logical execution unit. It gathers application blocks interacting with one or more physical processes [7]. These blocks may share data and also the command of a same physical process [5].

An IEC 61499 application is then a set of FBs distributed on several resources of devices. According to specifications, these blocks have to verify end to end response time bounds (denoted by eertb constraints). These bounds have to be respected between the receive of stimulus from sensors and the activation of the corresponding actuators [8].
Several works have been proposed to validate the tem- poral behavior of a FBs network [9, 10]. Nevertheless, they don't take into account characteristics of the execu- tion support.

In [11,12], we consider an already deployed application in distributed multi-tasking PLCs [13]. The main fea- ture of these controllers is the on-line preemptive schedul- ing of tasks. In this approach, one task is associated to one resource. Therefore, we consider these execution supports as multi-resources devices.
To validate the temporal behavior of such application, we have to check the feasibility in each device and also on the network connecting them.
Inside each device, we validate the temporal behavior of blocks by applying a hybrid approach. This approach combines off-line and on-line policies [11,12].

To check the on-line feasibility on the network [12], we generate a temporal characterization of exchanged mes- sages between devices. This characterization is based on the FBs execution. It allows to apply an existing schedu- lability condition checking their feasibility [14].
A hard point is how to deploy application FBs in a dis- tributed architecture ?
In this paper, we consider several constraints on the execution support and the application blocks.

We propose a characterization for each device. This characterization is in terms of maximum number of tasks allowed by the RTOS [15]. In addition to the eertb bounds, we consider two constraints on the application blocks: the exclusion constraint [16] and the localization one [17].

Based on an analysis of the FBs network, an exclusion constraint defines a set of application FBs. These blocks share data or the command of a same physical process. Therefore, they have to be executed in non-preemption.

By gathering FBs in exclusion sets, the application is considered then as a set of exclusion sets with precedence constraints. To satisfy the standard instructions, an ex- clusion set has to be deployed in only one resource of a device.
On the other hand, the localization constraint of an ex- clusion set defines the devices able to execute its FBs. These devices provide the required services for these blocks.

The tackled deployment problem is classically NPhard [18]. Some heuristic methods, simulated annealing and genetic algorithms have been proposed to address this problem [17,19]. As far as we know, only one approach is proposed to deploy tasks with precedence and exclusion constraints [16]. This approach proposes an algorithm to find a feasible non-preemptive (ie. a pre-run-time) schedule.

In this paper, we propose a recursive algorithm deploying an IEC 61499 application. This algorithm is based on the list heuristic [20]. It deploys step by step the generated exclusion sets of the application.

To deploy an exclusion set, the algorithm seeks a re- source able to gather its FBs while respecting localization and temporal constraints. A new resource can also be con- structed for this set if constraints on the execution support are satisfied. Finally, if the set cannot be deployed, then we apply a backtrack redeploying already deployed blocks.

In the next section, we detail the FBs standard. We present then a formal characterization of an IEC61499 application. In the section 4, we explain the hybrid approach validating its temporal behavior. Finally, we propose the deployment method of such application. 2 The IEC 61499 standard We present the main concepts of the IEC 61499 Func- tion Blocks standard [21,5].
To validate the temporal behavior of the application, we propose some extensions and assumptions to take into account in all the continuation.

div.head: Concepts
div.p: A function block (FB) (figure 1) is a unit of software providing functionalities of an IEC 61499 application. It is composed by an interface and an implementation [6].
The interface contains data/event inputs and outputs supporting interactions with the environment. Events are responsible for the activation of the FB while data contain valued information.
The implementation of the block contains algorithms to execute when the corresponding events occur.

The selection of an algorithm to execute is performed by a state machine called the execution control chart (ECC). The ECC is also responsible for sending output events at the end of the algorithm execution. In [22,23],
we described in detail the FB behavior.

In the standard, a control application is specified by a network of FBs. In this network, each FB event input (resp. output) is linked to an event output (resp. input) (scheduling, communications and process mapping) Figure 1. A function Block. by a channel. Otherwise, it corresponds to a global input (resp. output). Data inputs and outputs follow the same rules.

The execution support architecture is defined by a network of devices. A device is composed of one processing unit and interfaces (with sensors, actuators and the net- work). Moreover, it is characterized by logical execution unit(s) called resource(s) [7].

A resource gathers application FBs interacting with one or more physical processes. The standard imposes a non-preemptive execution between these blocks [7]. Due to this restriction, a mutual exclusion on the interaction with these processes does not have to be explicitly han- dled.

A resource contains and serves application FBs: it de- fines "the important boundary existing between what is within the scope of the IEC 61499 model and what is device (ie. OS) and networks (ie. communications proto- cols)" [7].
On the other hand, the standard defines (in a resource) particular FBs called Service Interface Function Blocks (SIFBs). In a resource, these blocks support interactions with outside [7].

div.head: Extensions and assumptions
div.p: To analyze a FB behavior, we need to characterize the corresponding algorithms by worst (resp, Best) case exe- cution times WCET (resp, BCET). Moreover, we consider that output events can be sent (by the ECC) simultane- ously or in exclusion according to specifications.
To validate the temporal behavior of the application, we only focus on the events flow. Therefore, we have to suppose a synchronization between events and data flows.
In this paper, we consider periodic global input events. According to [24], we characterize them by a release time r, a period p and a jitter j (the maximum deviation of the period).
Finally, we don't restrict our researches to a particular network of devices. For sake of simplicity, we suppose a bus network to connect them.

Running example. For all the continuation, we will follow the simple toy example depicted in thefigure 2. This example presents a control application to deploy in two devices. To simplify the problem, we suppose that the RTOS of each device allows two OS tasks at the maximum.
We particularly present the behavior of the function blocks FB1 and FB3.
When the ECC of FB1 selects an ie1 occurrence, it has to ask the processor to perform the corresponding al- gorithm. When the execution ends, the ECC sends oe1 and oe2 to respectively FB2 and FB3.

In the same way, when the ECC of FB3 selects an ie3 occurrence, it has to ask the processor to perform the cor- responding algorithm. At the execution end, it sends oe6 to FB5 or oe5 and oe4 to respectively FB6 and FB7.

div.head: Formal characterization of a FBs application
div.p: According to specifications, a distributed application has to respect eertb constraints between the receive of stimulus from sensors and the activation of the corresponding actuators.

To verify these constraints, we propose in [23] a transformation approach of this application into an actions system with precedence constraints. The purpose is to exploit classical results on the scheduling of real-time tasks [25].

div.head: Actions
div.p: An action act corresponds to a FB execution activated by an input event ie. This action is characterized by: * WCET(act) (resp, BCET(act)) : the WCET (resp, Best) of the algorithm corresponding to ie.
* pred(act) the action to execute in the application before the act execution. This action belongs to the FB producing the output event corresponding to ie.

* succ(act) : a set of actions sets. Each actions set cor- responds to a possible execution scenario (ie. only one actions set between all ones is performed). The actions of a set have to be executed once the execution of act is finished. These actions belong to FBs activated once the treatment corresponding to ie fin- ishes. * (r, j, p, d) : the three first parameters characterize the activation of act [24]. They should be processed while taking into account the execution of pred(act) [26]. The deadline d defines the latest completion date of the execution. To respect eertb constraints, it should be processed while taking into account the deadlines of act successors [26].

To respect eertb bounds, we propose in [23] a method processing deadlines for the different actions of the application traces. 4

div.head: Schedulability analysis
div.p: In [ 1], we consider an already deployed application in a network of devices. To guarantee its temporal correct- ness, we have to check the application feasibility in each device and also on the network.

div.head: Device temporal validation
div.p: We suppose in this section a multi-resources device. According to the standard [5], we have to apply a non- preemptive policy to schedule actions inside each re- source. Nevertheless, an on-line and preemptive policy is often required by several RTOSs [15].
To meet these requirements, we propose in [11,12] a hybrid scheduling approach combining off-line and on- line policies.

The off-line policy (i.e non-preemptive) allows to val- idate the temporal behavior inside each resource. If it is unfeasible, then we conclude as soon as possible that the application is also unfeasible. Otherwise, we generate a pre-scheduling [28].
To apply an on-line policy, we transform each generated pre-scheduling into an OS task [15].
Running example. To explain the hybrid approach, we suppose that the FBs: FB1, FB3, FB5, FB6 and FB7 are deployed in a same resource r of a device.

div.head: Schedulability analysis in a resource
div.p: To validate the temporal behavior inside a resource, we apply a schedulability analysis of the corresponding actions set a [23,22]. This analysis is based on the construc- tion of an accessibility graph in a hyper period [29]. If the system a is feasible, then we generate a static scheduling [29] to use by a sequencer at run-time [23].
This scheduling is a direct acyclic graph (DAG) where each trajectory is a possible execution scenario. A state of the graph specifies the execution start time of an action instance [23].
We consider the generated static scheduling as a prescheduling [28]. Indeed, the execution of a pre-scheduling may be preempted to execute a pre-scheduling of another resource.
The application blocks in the device are considered then as a set of pre-schedulings. Each pre-scheduling en- code the behavior of each resource.

Running example. In this example, we suppose that the resource r is feasible. We briefly present in the figure 3 the corresponding pre-scheduling. This pre-scheduling is a DAG where each trajectory is a possible execution scenario of r. Note that when the execution of act' ends, the sequencer has to execute act' or act'.

div.head: Transformation into OS tasks
div.p: If all resources are feasible, we transform the corresponding pre-schedulings into OS tasks [ 1].

By considering a conditional behavior of the application, we exploit the recurring real-time task model [30] to represent these pre-schedulings. This model is a generalization of all previous real-time task models. It was introduced to represent conditional real time codes [30].

A recurring task F is represented by a task graph G(F) and a period P(F). The task graph G(F) is a direct acyclic graph (DAG) with a unique source vertex and a unique Figure 4. a recurring task of a resource. sink vertex. Each vertex of this DAG represents a subtask and each edge represents a possible flow of control. Moreover, each subtask is characterized by a triggering time and a deadline.
The pre-scheduling of each resource is transformed then into a recurring task. The application blocks in the device are considered then as a set of OS tasks to on-line schedule.

This task is a DAG where each trajectory is a possible execution scenario ofr.

To reduce the on-line scheduling complexity, a tech- nique is proposed in [11] to merge several actions in- stances into only one subtask. For example, the subtask Ti implements the instances act' and act'.

div.head: On-line feasibility analysis
div.p: Once all the pre-schedulings are transformed into OS tasks, we analyze their on-line feasibility exploiting a schedulability condition proposed in [30]. This condition is checked in a proven hyper period [30].

div.head: Network validation
div.p: To validate the application behavior on the network, we check the feasibility of the exchanged messages between devices.

We propose in [12] a temporal characterization of these messages while basing on the FBs execution. This charac- Figure 3. a pre-scheduling of a resource. terization allows to apply an existing schedulability con- dition checking their feasibility [25,14].

div.head: Deployment method
div.p: In this paper, we suppose a not deployed application in the execution support. Therefore, we propose a static method [17] deploying its FBs in resources of devices.
Based on a heuristic, such deployment has to take into account constraints on the execution support and also on the application blocks.

div.head: Deployment constraints
div.p: In addition to the eertb bounds, we propose the following constraints to take into account during the deployment, Figure 6. Exclusion sets with precedence constraints.

div.head: Functional constraints
div.p: We consider two functional constraints: the exclusion and the localization constraints.

div.head: * Exclusion constraints
div.p: We consider that FBs are under an exclusion constraint [16] if they share data or also the command of a same physical process. Therefore, they should be executed in non-preemption. We propose to gather them in a logical container called an "exclusion set".
The application is considered then as a set of exclu- sion sets with precedence constraints. To reduce the deployment complexity, we propose to consider ex- clusions sets instead of FBs.
On the other hand, the standard allows only non- preemptive execution inside a resource [5,7]. There- fore, we propose to deploy each exclusion set in only one resource of a device.
We denote by Excl the set of all the exclusion sets of the application (cardinality(Excl) = n).

div.head: * Localization constraints
div.p: In this paper, we consider for each exclusion set a localization constraint.
The localization of a set e (denoted by Local (e) ) is the set of devices able to execute its FBs. These devices provide the required services for these blocks.

div.head: Execution support constraints
div.p: According to [15], the RTOS of a device dev allows a maximum number of OS tasks to schedule. We denote by max (dev) such number. By considering the hybrid approach, the number of resources to construct in each device dev does not have to exceed max (dev).
Running example. We suppose the following exclu- sion and localization constraints on the application blocks (figure 5).
The application is considered then as a set ofexclusion sets with precedence constraints (figure 6).

div.head: Deployment heuristic
div.p: The tackled problem of the application deployment is classically NP-hard [18]. Therefore, we exploit the list heuristic to perform such deployment [20].
This heuristic attributes a priority level for each exclusion set. The deployment of a set is done only if all ones with higher priorities are deployed.
Several subclasses of this heuristic have been proposed. We use in this paper the HLFET as a BNP scheduling al- gorithm [20].

By considering exclusion sets with precedence con- straints, this algorithm processes for them static priority levels (b-levels). The b-level of a set ei is the length of the longest path from ei to an exit set (with no successor). To compute these levels, we attribute for each set ei a weight equal to the WCET of all its FBs actions. Note that we can use other heuristic algorithms based on dynamic priority levels [20]. Indeed, the deployment method that we propose is independant of the chosen algorithm.
For all the continuation, we denote by el .1...... e,ethe exclusion sets of Excl in the descending order of priorities.
Running Example. In this example, the ascending order of indexing is the descending priority order (ie. iec has the highest priority).

div.head: Deployment steps
div.p: To deploy the application, we seek for each set ei, i E [1, n] the resource able to contain its blocks while respecting the corresponding constraints.
If a set cannot be deployed, then we apply a backtrack to redeploy previously deployed sets. We propose the following steps to apply recursively for each set ei, i E [1,n].
Step 1.
In each device device(ei) E local(ei), we seek an al- ready constructed resource able to contain this set.
A resource is able to contain ei if a static scheduling of its exclusion sets including ei is feasible.
If no resources of device(ei) are able to contain ei and if their number is lower than max(device(ej)), then we construct a new resource gathering ei.
Finally, note that if we cannot deploy ei in any device belonging to local(ei), then we perform a backtrack to redeploy previous deployed sets (ie. ej, j C [1, i -1]).
Step 2.
We denote by res the resource of device(ei) able to contain the set ei. We transform the static scheduling of res (including ei) into a recurring task.
To guarantee the correct behavior of device(ei) and also of the communication network, we verify the on-line feasibility of, * The OS tasks in device(ei).
* The exchanged messages between the already de- ployed sets including ei (ie. ej, j C [0, i]).
If the verification is failed, then we re-apply the Step 1 to deploy ei in another resource.

div.head: Conclusion
div.p: This paper proposes an approach deploying an IEC 61499 application in a network of devices. A device is characterized by a constraint in terms of the maximum number of tasks allowed by the RTOS.

According to specifications, the application FBs have to respect end to end response time bounds. In The application is considered then as a set of exclusion sets with precedence constraints. Each set contains blocks sharing data or the command of a same physical process.

The deployment problem of the application is classically NP-hard. Therefore, we use a heuristic processing different priority levels for its exclusion sets. The deployment of each set is allowed if all ones with higher priorities are deployed.

To deploy an exclusion set, we seek the resource able to gather its blocks while respecting corresponding con- straints. If a set cannot be deployed, then a backtrack is performed to redeploy sets with higher priorities.

In our future works, we plan to consider other con- straints to take into account. The response time minimiza- tion, the resources number minimization, the memories size minimization and the energy consumption minimiza- tion have to be studied.
On the other hand, the use of a heuristic with dynamic priorities should be also analyzed. Indeed, the priorities change may be needed during the deployment of exclusion sets.

Finally, we plan to propose a method generating SIFBs for resources. The purpose is to optimize services for application blocks. This method has also to implement the devices interfaces with physical processes and the com- munication network.
